toc.title: Define a Communication Strategy (ECO) = Plan Communications Management
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Purpose: an efficient and effective information flow between the project team and stakeholders, with the right information reaching the right people at the right time in a form they can use. Much of project work is engaging and communicating with stakeholders.

Term Meaning
Communications management plan Describes how, when and by whom information will be administered and disseminated; how communications are planned, structured, implemented and monitored for effectiveness. Both an input (who gets what, when, how) and a living output
Stakeholder communication requirements The information each stakeholder needs, in what format and detail, and how often
Categories of information Internal or external, sensitive or public, general or detailed
Project communications Performance reports, deliverable status, schedule progress, costs incurred, presentations and other information stakeholders need
Status report Current status of the project: progress since the last report and forecasts for cost and schedule
Work performance reports Compiled work performance information intended to generate decisions, actions or awareness (status and progress reports; EV graphs, trend lines, burndown charts, defect histograms, risk summaries); shown as dashboards, heat reports or stoplight charts
Project reporting Collecting and distributing project information, adapted in level, format and detail for each type of stakeholder; regular or exception-based
Interactive / push / pull communication Real-time multidirectional exchange / sent to specific recipients / accessed by recipients at their discretion
Communication channels The potential paths between people: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many (section 4)
Noise Anything that interferes with a message: distraction, barriers, differing perceptions, inadequate technology
Feedback Information about reactions to communications, a deliverable or a situation; supports interactive communication (coaching, mentoring, negotiating are examples)
Information radiator A visible, physical (often low-tech) display placed where people can see it; also "big visible chart"; easy to update and updated often
Escalation Moving a matter to a higher authority when it exceeds the team's authority or cannot be resolved (defined in the plan)

2The Three Communication Processes

Process Focus area Purpose Key outputs Decision tools
Plan Communications Management Planning Plan how to communicate with identified stakeholders inside and outside the team; overlaps with stakeholder identification, analysis and engagement and stays consistent with the stakeholder engagement plan Communications management plan, stakeholder engagement plan updates Communication requirements analysis, technology, models, methods, styles assessment, political and cultural awareness, stakeholder engagement assessment matrix, meetings
Manage Communications Executing Set up and conduct communications: timely and appropriate collection, creation, distribution, storage, retrieval, management, monitoring and disposition of project information; stay flexible as needs change Project communications, plan updates, issue and lessons learned updates Communication technology and methods, communication competence, feedback, nonverbal communication, presentations, PMIS, project reporting, active listening, conflict and meeting management, networking
Monitor Communications Monitoring & Controlling Make sure the information needs of the project and its stakeholders are met; optimal flow as defined in the communications and stakeholder engagement plans Work performance information, change requests, plan and document updates Expert judgment, PMIS, stakeholder engagement assessment matrix, observation and conversation, meetings

3Define a Communication Strategy (ECO) = Plan Communications Management

Steps:

  1. Analyze stakeholders and their information needs (stakeholder register and engagement plan, Topic 13).
  2. Perform communication requirements analysis: interviews, workshops, lessons learned from earlier projects. Sources: stakeholder register and engagement plan, number of potential channels, organization charts, responsibilities and interdependencies, development approach, disciplines and locations, internal and external needs (media, public, contractors), legal requirements. Combine the type and format of information with the value of that information.
  3. Categorize information (internal or external, sensitive or public, general or detailed) and decide who may release confidential information.
  4. Choose methods and technology for each audience and message (section 5).
  5. Define content, level of detail, frequency, owner, escalation, resources and templates in the communications management plan.
  6. Tailor and keep it alive: review it periodically and revise it as the stakeholder community, phase, team structure or environment changes. Complex projects with many stakeholders need a more sophisticated plan.

Factors in choosing communication technology: urgency of the information; availability and reliability of the technology; ease of use (and training); the project environment (face-to-face or virtual, time zones, languages, culture); sensitivity and confidentiality (security measures, social media policies).

Tailoring to the audience (PMBOK 8): use different methods (email for formal updates, messaging for quick questions, feedback loops, face-to-face meetings) and different levels of detail per stakeholder role.

4Communication Models, Channels and Methods

  • Basic sender-receiver model: encode, transmit through a medium, decode. It checks that the message was delivered, not that it was understood.
  • Interactive model: adds acknowledgment and feedback/response. The receiver acknowledging receipt does not mean agreement or comprehension. If the sender sees that the feedback matches the original message, communication succeeded.
  • Responsibilities: the sender transmits clearly and completely and confirms correct interpretation; the receiver receives all of it, interprets it correctly and acknowledges or responds.
  • Both sides are shaped by emotional state, knowledge, background, personality, culture (generational, national, professional discipline, gender) and biases. Cross-cultural communication adds language, style and protocol differences.
  • The model suits person-to-person or small-group communication, not emails, broadcasts or social media.

Common barriers and the usual fix [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]:

Barrier Typical sign Fix
Information overload The one decision needed is on slide 31 of a 40-slide pack Lead with the decision or ask; summarize; one message, one purpose
Filtering A team lead softens bad news before it reaches the sponsor Create a safe channel; ask for facts and options, not only status
Jargon "Done" means merged to one team and released to another Define terms or use plain language; check understanding
Cultural difference A direct "no" is rude in one culture, while hedged wording is read as agreement in another Clarify meaning, ask for confirmation, learn the norms
Wrong medium A safety notice goes by email to crews with no email access on site Fit the channel to the receiver and the urgency

Method Description Example artifacts
Interactive Multidirectional, real time Meetings, calls, instant messaging, videoconferencing
Push Sent to recipients; ensures distribution, not receipt or understanding Letters, memos, reports, email, press releases
Pull Accessed at the recipient's discretion; for large, complex information or large audiences Web portals, intranets, e-learning, lessons learned databases, repositories

Forms: interpersonal, small group (three to six people), public, mass, and networks or social computing (many-to-many).

Channels formula [Beyond PMBOK 8]: channels = n × (n − 1) ÷ 2. Ten people have 45 channels; twelve have 66; twenty have 190. PMBOK 8 asks you to consider the number of potential channels in communication requirements analysis.

5Promote Transparency and Collaboration (ECO)

Practice How it helps
Make information visible where stakeholders can reach it Information radiators, dashboards, shared backlogs and boards, pull repositories; an information radiator hidden in the team's room does not create transparency
Report honestly and early PMBOK 8 treats integrity as sharing risks, assumptions and basis of estimates, delivering bad news early and keeping status reports accurate; also disclose conflicts of interest (Topic 06)
Create a safe, open environment Open and safe communication is a feature of high-performing teams; positive discourse means dialogue, not win-lose debate; support, courage and celebrating success keep the team communicating
Build regular collaboration into the rhythm Daily coordination meetings, planning, reviews and retrospectives; virtual collaboration tools (cloud platforms for real-time work)
Engage people in the way that suits them Written or asynchronous input for those who prefer it; multilingual updates and virtual forums on global projects
Use storytelling Conveys lessons, good practice and outcomes in a relatable way; effective for tacit knowledge and culture
Respect confidentiality The plan names who may release confidential information; apply security and policy limits

6Establish a Feedback Loop (ECO)

  • Plan feedback channels: sprint or iteration reviews with structured feedback time, retrospectives, interviews and surveys, one-to-one conversations, demonstrations, stakeholder engagement assessment matrix, indicators such as Net Promoter Score (PMBOK 8 Table 2-9).
  • Use active listening: acknowledge, clarify, confirm, understand and address barriers; essential in global and cross-cultural settings.
  • Confirm understanding: a message acknowledged but not acted on correctly shows the link in the loop failed; switch to interactive communication (conversation, demonstration) and check what was understood.
  • Recurring misunderstanding despite repeated clarifications: find the root cause (why is it being misread?) rather than sending more of the same messages.
  • Bring the actual audience into the loop: external customers or end users, not only internal proxies, in reviews.
  • Monitor Communications: check whether the information flow meets the needs (stakeholder engagement assessment matrix, observation and conversation, meetings); adjust methods, frequency and content; update the plan; raise change requests when needed.
  • Act on feedback visibly: close the loop by telling people what changed as a result.

Situations that test the loop [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]:

Situation Best response
Messages are consistent and accurate, yet recipients keep hearing news from other sources first The fault is timing and channel, not content: revise the communication strategy to reach them sooner, where they actually look. Longer notices or extra approvals do not fix it
A group receives your updates but never responds; the plan assumed silence means agreement Silence is not agreement. Find a channel and format that draws feedback from that group (short call, drop-in, survey, a named contact). A reply deadline or a "low interest" label does not
Decisions are made in ad hoc calls and the notes sit in personal folders Agree one shared, visible place where decisions are recorded (decision log, team site). More emailed notes or limiting decisions to scheduled meetings scatters or slows the team

7Reporting: Requirements, Alignment and Governance (ECO)

7.1 Understand reporting requirements

Ask: who needs what, for which decision, how often, in which format? Sources: sponsor expectations, the governance framework and escalation thresholds (Topic 12), contracts, regulators, the PMO and organizational policies, and the information requirements identified in planning (Topic 14, section 5).

7.2 Create reports aligned with sponsors and stakeholders

  • Tailor level, format and detail to each audience. One long report rarely serves both an executive (summary, outcomes, forecasts, key risks and decisions needed) and an engineer (detail). Use summaries, dashboards, detailed boards or exception reports as appropriate.
  • Dashboards: charts and graphs of progress against key measures, often stoplight (red-amber-green) charts, bar, pie and control charts; add a text explanation for any measure outside its thresholds; drill-down for detail.
  • Work performance reports: status or progress reports with EV graphs, trend lines and forecasts, burndown or burnup charts, defect histograms, contract performance and risk summaries (Topic 28).
  • Standardize inputs at the source when the reporting requirement is fixed (for example a data template aligned to the sponsor's format) instead of re-mapping each submission every period.
  • Be accurate and timely; report on schedule or by exception, include forecasts, and escalate per the plan.
  • Agile: transparency through visible boards, burn charts and information radiators; a burnup that shows scope growth explains why completion moves; do not let it look like a slow team.

7.3 Support reporting and governance

  • If governance asks for specific information (for example earned value), adapt the reporting to provide it; the project does not decide whether the requirement is needed.
  • When several oversight bodies request different formats and frequencies, agree one reporting structure with them (through the sponsor) and a single source of truth, then create tailored views, instead of building separate ad hoc reports for each.
  • Keep project artifacts accessible and controlled (one repository, approved versions) so auditors and stakeholders find the same data (Topic 28).
  • Record the reporting design in the communications management plan and review it periodically.

8Communication Skills, Awareness and Meetings

  • Communication competence combines tailored skills with clarity of purpose, effective relationships and information sharing, and leadership behavior.
  • Skills: oral (interaction, presentation, active listening, meeting facilitation), visual (data visualization, nonverbal communication), electronic (writing, email, texting, chat, AI prompts).
  • Nonverbal communication: gestures, tone of voice, facial expressions, mirroring, eye contact; be aware of what you say and do not say.
  • Communication styles assessment: find each stakeholder's preferred method, format and content; often used with unsupportive stakeholders after a stakeholder engagement assessment.
  • Cultural awareness: adapt the strategy to differences among individuals, groups and organizations. Political awareness: recognize formal and informal power relationships and communicate with those who hold power.
  • Presentations: formal delivery of information that works when content and delivery fit the audience's expectations and needs as well as the project's.
  • Meetings: types include decision-making, facilitated workshops, issue resolution, lessons learned and retrospectives, kickoffs, sprint planning and status updates. Meeting management steps: distribute an agenda stating objectives; start and finish on time; invite and ensure the right participants; stay on topic; manage expectations, issues and conflicts; record actions with owners.
  • Daily coordination meeting (agile): short (no more than 15 minutes); progress since yesterday, plan for today, obstacles; builds accountability and self-direction. It is for the team, not a status report to the project manager.
  • AI in communications (PMBOK 8): assess AI use through a decision process; consider security and ethics (for example involve cybersecurity); review AI-drafted artifacts for accuracy and bias; avoid placing confidential project data in unapproved tools (Topic 08).

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Plan Formal communications management plan: matrix of audiences, content, timing, owners Light plan plus working agreements; communication built into events Formal plan for governance and customers; team rhythm inside
Information flow Scheduled status reports, newsletters, town halls, formal change communications Continuous feedback: daily coordination, sprint reviews and retrospectives, shared boards Both
Transparency Reports and dashboards to governance Information radiators, burn charts, open backlog Dashboards for sponsors, boards for the team
Feedback Interviews, surveys, review meetings Feedback in every review and retrospective; customers in the room Both
Reporting to executives Status report with forecasts Burn charts and release forecasts; milestones with iterations beneath Milestone view with iteration detail underneath
Beyond PMBOK 8 Asynchronous and written input to include quieter voices

10Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

Tailoring considerations (PMBOK 8 §2.5.3): organizational culture (flat organizations rely on open, informal channels; hierarchical ones use formal approaches); product (iterative or exploratory products bring events such as product reviews, planning sessions and retrospectives); AI and large language models (assess use, include security and ethics); stakeholder variety, project size and complexity.

PMBOK 8 examples: (1) an agile project needs continuous feedback, so daily coordination meetings and dedicated platforms support real-time collaboration; (2) a large ERP rollout in manufacturing sends biweekly email newsletters and monthly town halls for alignment across hierarchical levels; (3) a medium-sized global project uses multilingual updates and monthly virtual forums for inclusive engagement.

Interactions: communications link to stakeholder engagement (same analysis), governance (reporting), risk (stakeholder communication about risks and issues), schedule (communication activities and meetings), resources (team communication, virtual teams) and quality and scope (acceptance and feedback).

Check results (Table 2-9):

Outcome Check
Stakeholder engagement maintained Feedback through interviews and surveys, periodic alignment on objectives, indicators such as NPS
Communications management performed Review the communications management plan periodically and tailor it to stakeholders' needs
Agreement with project objectives Number of change requests to requirements; feedback on increments

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Find out what each stakeholder needs before writing the plan: communication requirements analysis, not assumptions.
  2. Tailor reports to the audience; one size does not fit both executives and engineers.
  3. Acknowledgment is not understanding. Check understanding with interactive communication and feedback.
  4. When clarifications keep failing, find the root cause instead of sending the message again.
  5. Pull for large, evolving information; push for key alerts; interactive for complex or sensitive matters.
  6. Transparency means information is accessible to the stakeholders, not just posted in the team's own space.
  7. Deliver bad news early, factually, with impact and options; keep status reports accurate.
  8. Support governance: give the board the information it requires; agree one reporting structure when several bodies ask for different formats.
  9. Standardize data at the source when a reporting format is fixed.
  10. Feedback needs room: sprint reviews should include structured discussion time and the real customers, not proxies.
  11. Adapt to culture: use cultural awareness, one-to-one or written follow-up, and confirmation of understanding; do not rely on public agreement.
  12. Channels grow quickly with team size (n(n − 1) ÷ 2): add structure, tools and smaller teams.
  13. Keep the communications management plan current and review it periodically.
  14. Meetings need an agenda, timing, the right people and recorded actions; a daily coordination meeting is short and for the team.
  15. Use AI carefully: assess it, protect confidential data and verify its output.
  16. Confidential information is released only by the person authorized in the plan.
  17. Silence is not agreement, and consistent content can still fail. Change the channel, timing or format until feedback flows, and record decisions in one shared, visible place.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A program team of 10 people will grow to 15 members. By how many do the potential communication channels increase?

  • ABy 23, because channels grow by the same 50% as the team does
  • BBy 5, because one channel is added for each of the five new members
  • CBy 50, because each new member adds a channel to each existing member only
  • DBy 60, as channels rise from 45 to 105 when the team grows to 15
Show the answer

Answer: D. Potential channels equal n times (n minus 1) divided by 2: 10 people have 45 channels and 15 people have 105, an increase of 60. Adding one channel per person, or miscalculating the starting figure, understates or distorts the growth.

S2Four hundred stakeholders across several countries need access to a large set of procurement documents that are updated several times a week. Which communication method fits best?

  • APush, emailing every updated document to all four hundred stakeholders at once
  • BPull, using a portal or repository that stakeholders access at their own discretion
  • CInteractive, calling each stakeholder whenever a document is changed
  • DPush, mailing a printed copy of the full set once a month to each stakeholder
Show the answer

Answer: B. Pull communication suits large, complex or frequently updated information and large audiences, because people retrieve what they need when they need it. Push sends information without ensuring it is received or understood, and interactive contact does not scale to this audience.

S3A distributed scrum team confirms by email that it received the new reporting rules, yet its first reports use the old format. Which statement about communication does this best illustrate?

  • AA confirmed delivery shows that the sender's message was fully understood
  • BAcknowledging receipt does not mean the receiver understood or agreed
  • CUnderstanding is the responsibility of the receiver alone, not the sender
  • DEmail is always an effective method for passing on new rules to a team
Show the answer

Answer: B. In the interactive model, an acknowledgment shows only that the message arrived; the sender confirms interpretation through feedback or a conversation. Both sender and receiver share responsibility, and no single method guarantees understanding.

S4The communications plan for an agile product was copied from a larger earlier predictive project, and stakeholders now complain of irrelevant emails while missing the updates they need. What should the project manager do?

  • ASend a reminder that the plan was approved and ask people to follow its schedule
  • BSwitch every update to a weekly summary report written for the sponsor
  • CAnalyze communication requirements with the stakeholders, then update the plan
  • DAdd more recipients to every update so that nobody is left out
Show the answer

Answer: C. A communications plan rests on analysis of what each stakeholder needs, in what format and how often, and it is revised as the community changes. Defending the plan, copying more people or writing only for the sponsor skips that analysis.

S5A journalist phones a team member for details of a contract dispute on the project. What should the team member do, according to a well-prepared communications plan?

  • AHang up and tell nobody about the call to avoid spreading rumors
  • BRefer the journalist to the person authorized to release project information
  • CAnswer the questions briefly, since honesty is the best policy with the media
  • DShare only the documents that are already marked as public on the portal
Show the answer

Answer: B. Confidential and sensitive information is released only by the person authorized in the communications management plan, so the caller is referred on and the project manager is told. Answering, hiding the call or choosing documents personally bypasses that control.

S6The weekly coordination meetings of a hybrid program run for two hours with no agenda, and actions agreed in them are rarely carried out. What should the project manager change first?

  • ALengthen the meetings so that every agenda item can be discussed fully
  • BCancel the status meetings and ask for written updates from each member
  • CInvite more participants so that nobody can claim to have missed a decision
  • DSet an agenda with objectives, invite the right people and record actions with owners
Show the answer

Answer: D. Effective meetings have an agenda stating objectives, start and finish on time, the right participants, a focus on the topics and recorded actions with owners. Canceling, lengthening or inviting more people does not give the meetings structure.

S7A local lead in a hierarchical culture agrees to every proposal in video sprint-planning sessions, yet later voices concerns privately to a colleague. How should the project manager adapt?

  • AReplace the lead with someone who is more comfortable disagreeing in public
  • BTreat the public agreement as final and move on to the next agenda item
  • CAsk the lead to state objections openly in front of the whole group
  • DFollow up one-to-one or in writing, and confirm understanding and concerns
Show the answer

Answer: D. Cultural awareness means adapting the strategy so that concerns surface: one-to-one or written follow-up and a check of understanding, rather than relying on public agreement. Accepting it, forcing open objection or replacing the lead ignores the cultural difference.

S8A sponsor sees a dashboard with five red indicators and no explanation, and asks what is wrong. What should the project manager have added to the dashboard?

  • AA text explanation for each measure outside its threshold
  • BA note telling the sponsor to ask the team about any red indicator
  • CA weekly summary of the number of meetings held and emails sent
  • DMore indicators in green so that the dashboard looks balanced overall
Show the answer

Answer: A. Dashboards show progress against key measures, usually in red, amber and green, and add a text explanation for any measure outside its thresholds, with drill-down for detail. Padding with green indicators, activity counts or a request to ask the team does not inform decisions.

S9New staff at a remote site need to understand the culture and the hard-won lessons behind the project's working methods, which are not written down. Which technique conveys this best?

  • AAn email with a link to the project schedule and the work breakdown structure
  • BA detailed policy manual that lists every rule of the working methods
  • CStorytelling, which conveys tacit knowledge and lessons in a relatable way
  • DA dashboard of key performance indicators updated at the end of each week
Show the answer

Answer: C. Storytelling conveys lessons, good practice and culture, especially tacit knowledge, in a way people remember and relate to. A rule manual, a schedule link or a dashboard conveys explicit data, not the experience behind it.

S10A resistant stakeholder never answers the project's emails, and a stakeholder engagement assessment shows the person is far below the desired engagement level. What should the project manager do?

  • AMark the stakeholder as low interest and stop sending updates
  • BSend the same emails more often and copy the stakeholder's manager
  • CAssess the person's communication style and use the preferred channel and format
  • DWait until the stakeholder raises a complaint through the formal channel
Show the answer

Answer: C. A communication styles assessment finds each stakeholder's preferred method, format and content, and is often used with unsupportive stakeholders after an engagement assessment. Repeating the failed channel, dropping the stakeholder or waiting for a complaint does not close the gap.

S11The stakeholder Net Promoter Score has fallen from 40 to 15 over two quarters, while status reports remain on time and accurate. What should the project manager do?

  • ATalk with stakeholders to learn why, then adjust the approach
  • BIgnore the score, since the reports are on time and accurate
  • CReplace the survey with one that asks only about the reports' accuracy
  • DSend longer reports so that stakeholders have more information to read
Show the answer

Answer: A. A falling score is a feedback signal that the information flow or engagement is not meeting needs, so the project manager asks stakeholders what changed and adapts the approach. Ignoring it, adding length or narrowing the survey hides the feedback.

S12A change to a safety procedure must reach 60 site supervisors today, and the project manager must be sure they have understood it. Which combination is best?

  • AA push alert, then a short interactive briefing to confirm understanding
  • BA push alert only, since the supervisors will respond if they have questions
  • CA formal letter to each supervisor's line manager within the next two weeks
  • DA pull posting on the intranet, assuming supervisors will find and read it
Show the answer

Answer: A. Push ensures that a key alert is distributed quickly, and interactive communication checks understanding for matters that are important or sensitive. A pull posting, an alert alone or a slow letter does not both reach and confirm understanding today.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1Name the three communication processes.

Show the answer

Plan Communications Management, Manage Communications, Monitor Communications.

R2What does the communications management plan describe?

Show the answer

How, when and by whom information is administered and disseminated, including requirements, content, format, timing, responsible persons, recipients, methods, resources, escalation, update method, glossary, information flows and constraints.

R3Give examples of interactive, push and pull communication.

Show the answer

Interactive: meetings, calls, instant messaging, videoconferencing. Push: letters, memos, reports, email. Pull: portals, intranets, e-learning, knowledge repositories.

R4What is the communication channels formula?** **[Beyond PMBOK 8]

Show the answer

n × (n − 1) ÷ 2; for example 10 people have 45 channels.

R5Basic versus interactive communication model?

Show the answer

The basic model (encode, transmit, decode) checks delivery; the interactive model adds acknowledgment and feedback to check understanding. Acknowledgment confirms receipt, not agreement.

R6What is communication requirements analysis?

Show the answer

Determining stakeholders' information needs (type, format and value) through interviews, workshops and lessons learned, using sources such as the stakeholder register, organization charts, channels, development approach and legal requirements.

R7What categories of information does PMBOK 8 mention?

Show the answer

Internal or external, sensitive or public, general or detailed.

R8Name the forms of communication.

Show the answer

Interpersonal, small group (three to six people), public, mass, and networks or social computing.

R9What does active listening involve?

Show the answer

Acknowledging, clarifying, confirming, understanding and addressing barriers to communication.

R10What is a project dashboard?

Show the answer

A set of charts and graphs (often red-amber-green, bar, pie, control charts) showing progress against key measures, with explanatory text for measures outside thresholds.

R11What is an information radiator?

Show the answer

A visible, physical display placed where people can see it (a big visible chart), easy to update and updated frequently.

R12List the steps of meeting management.

Show the answer

Agenda with objectives, start and finish on time, the right participants, stay on topic, manage expectations and conflicts, and record actions with owners.

R13What are the rules of a daily coordination meeting?

Show the answer

Brief (no more than 15 minutes); progress since the previous day, plan for the day and obstacles; builds accountability and team self-direction.

R14Cultural awareness versus political awareness?

Show the answer

Cultural awareness adapts communication to cultural differences; political awareness recognizes formal and informal power relationships and communicates accordingly.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Processes Plan Communications Mgmt → Manage Communications → Monitor Communications (Stakeholders domain)

Requirements analysis Interviews, workshops, lessons learned; stakeholder register; channels; development approach; legal needs

Feedback loop Review feedback time, retrospectives, surveys, NPS; active listening; adjust and tell people what changed
Reporting Know requirements; tailor level, format, detail; dashboards with explanations; exception reporting
Governance Provide what governance requires; agree one reporting structure and a single data source
